explainBack.question: Why does the House passing H.R. 9340 by 417–3 not change what any household pays for electricity this month?
explainBack.answer: Because a one-chamber vote is only a proposal: the bill takes effect only if the Senate passes it and it is enacted. Even then, it would not set a rate itself — it would require each state regulator and nonregulated utility to commence consideration of a standard for computing sites with at least 100 MW of peak demand and make a determination. Household bills would change only after enactment, a local proceeding, and an approved rate design; a Senate unanimous-consent attempt already drew an objection on September 17.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The answer should name the enactment gap (Senate objection, no established Senate vote), the 'consider a standard' mechanism rather than a nationwide rate, the 100 MW qualifying threshold, and the dependence on local regulator decisions.
explainBack.assessment: The article supports every element of this answer in P002's Washington section and P003's decision-chain summary, so the mechanism survives explain-back accurately in ordinary language.
